title: Gravitational Force
seo_title: Gravitational Force Worksheets: Newton's Law of Gravitation and Inverse Squares (Physics)
standard_text: Use mathematical representations of Newton's Law of Gravitation and Coulomb's Law to describe and predict the gravitational and electrostatic forces between objects.
meta_desc: Free high school physics worksheets on gravitational force (NGSS HS-PS2-4): Newton's law of gravitation, the inverse-square law, weight on other planets and orbits. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: F = Gm₁m₂/r²: more mass, more force; twice the distance, 1/4 the force.
body_html:
How to think about it

Every two masses attract: F = Gm1m2 ÷ r2.

  • Double one mass → double the force. Double the distance → 1/4 the force (inverse square).
  • G = 6.67 × 10−11 N·m²/kg², so the force between small objects is tiny.
  • Weight W = mg depends on the planet; mass does not change.
Example

Distance tripled. Force?

1 ÷ 3²

Answer: 1/9 as large

Example

70 kg on Mars (g = 3.7)?

70 × 3.7

Answer: 259 N

Common mistakes

  • Thinking doubling the distance halves the force.
  • Thinking there is no gravity in space.
  • Thinking mass changes on another planet.

faq.q: What is Newton's law of universal gravitation?
faq.a: Every two masses attract each other with a force F = Gm₁m₂/r², where r is the distance between their centers.

faq.q: What happens if the distance doubles?
faq.a: The gravitational force becomes 1/4 as large because it depends on 1 ÷ r².

faq.q: Why do astronauts float in orbit?
faq.a: Gravity still pulls on them, but they and their spacecraft are falling around Earth together.
